title: Array Reduce Transformation
statement:
Write `reduce(nums, fn, init)`, which combines the integer array `nums` into a single value using the reducer function `fn`. Keep a running value that starts as `init`. Go through `nums` from the first element to the last, and at each element replace the running value with `fn(running value, element)`: first `fn(init, nums[0])`, then `fn(that result, nums[1])`, and so on. Return the running value once every element has been used. When `nums` is empty, `fn` is never called and the answer is `init`.

Do not use the built-in `Array.prototype.reduce`: here it throws an error while your function runs.

Your function receives a real function as `fn`. In a case, `fn` is written as the name of one of these reducers, each called as `fn(accum, curr)`:

- `"sum"` returns `accum + curr`.
- `"sumOfSquares"` returns `accum + curr * curr`.
- `"zero"` returns `0`.
- `"max"` returns the larger of `accum` and `curr`.
- `"hash"` returns `(accum * 31 + curr) % 1000000007`.
- `"last"` returns `curr`.

Each case gives `nums`, `fn` and `init`, and the answer is the number your function returns.
signature: int reduce(int[] nums, String fn, int init)
api: reduce(nums: number[], fn: (accum: number, curr: number) => number, init: number): number
notes:
## Intuition

`reduce` is a **higher-order function**: it receives the reducer `fn` as an ordinary value and decides when to call it, while `fn` decides how two values combine. All `reduce` has to do is carry one running value through the array, from left to right, letting `fn` turn the old value and the next element into the new value. (The brute force states the same idea recursively: the result for the first `k` elements is `fn` applied to the result for the first `k - 1` elements and element `k - 1`, and the result for no elements is `init`.)

## Approach

1. Set `accum = init`.
2. For each index `i` from `0` to `nums.length - 1`, take `curr = nums[i]` and set `accum = fn(accum, curr)`.
3. Return `accum`. For an empty array the loop never runs, so the answer is `init`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]`, `fn` is `"sum"`, `init = 0`.

- `accum` starts at `0`.
- `curr = 1`: `fn(0, 1)` is `1`.
- `curr = 2`: `fn(1, 2)` is `3`.
- `curr = 3`: `fn(3, 3)` is `6`.
- `curr = 4`: `fn(6, 4)` is `10`, which is returned.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n) calls of `fn`, one per element (each reducer here is O(1)).
- Space: O(1) besides the input: only the running value is kept.

## Pitfalls

- Starting from `nums[0]` instead of `init` ignores `init`, so Example 2 gives `30` instead of `130`, and an empty array breaks.
- The order of the arguments matters: `fn(accum, curr)`, not `fn(curr, accum)`. With `"last"` or `"hash"` the swap gives a different answer.
- Walking the array from right to left changes the result for order-sensitive reducers such as `"hash"`.
- The built-in `nums.reduce(fn, init)` is not allowed here, and it throws while your function runs.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `accum` | the running value: `init` at first, then each result of `fn` |
| `i` | index of the element being combined |
| `curr` | the element `nums[i]` passed to `fn` |
| `fn` | the reducer that combines `accum` and `curr` |

narration.1: reduce receives the array, the reducer function fn and the starting value init.
narration.2: The running value starts as init; for an empty array it is also the answer.
narration.3: Visit the elements from first to last; the order matters for most reducers.
narration.4: curr is the element being combined in this step.
narration.5: Call fn with the running value and the element; its result becomes the new running value.
narration.7: After the last element, accum holds the final result.
